words.intro: The medical leaflet in every box of tablets is a work of German prose. It lists every possible side effect, down to one in ten thousand, and leaves readers feeling that the disease might have been safer.

grammar[0].fact: The zu-form in front of a noun is a German speciality: *die zu lösende Aufgabe*, the task to be solved. English needs five words where it has three, and it’s the first thing to go when a German writes well. You’ll still meet it in every form you fill in.

document.intro: A real package leaflet, folded and refolded. This corner says what the tablet looks like, how it’s sold and who makes it. Look at *erhältlich*, at the passive *in den Verkehr gebracht*, and at *zugelassen*.
document.fact: A German medicine must by law show every side effect, so the leaflet is long, but there is a rule that it must be understandable. It has to be tested on real readers before approval.
document.tasks[1].items[1].prompt: Es werden möglicherweise nicht alle Größen in den Verkehr gebracht.
reading.intro: Frau Huber has been given a small white tablet, for her blood pressure. She has read the leaflet, all four pages of it. Now she’s back at the surgery, with the leaflet, a ruler and a list. Dr. Weber’s next patient is waiting.
reading.fact: The frequency words on German package leaflets are official: *sehr häufig* means more than 1 in 10, *selten* less than 1 in 1,000, *sehr selten* less than 1 in 10,000. Most readers hugely overestimate them. Every medicine advertisement must end with the same rapid sentence, telling you to read the leaflet and to ask your doctor or pharmacist.
